content: Ariboflavinosis is a medical condition that arises due to a deficiency of riboflavin, also known as vitamin B2. This condition is frequently observed in individuals suffering from protein-energy malnutrition and is also commonly associated with chronic alcoholism. Historically, it was referred to as pellagra sin pellagra because it shares certain clinical similarities with pellagra, a condition caused by niacin deficiency. The primary cause of riboflavin deficiency is an inadequate dietary intake. Populations that consume limited amounts of riboflavin-rich foods, such as meats, eggs, milk, cheese, yogurt, leafy green vegetables, and whole grains, are at the highest risk. Additionally, individuals with impaired liver function may experience difficulty in properly utilizing riboflavin, further predisposing them to deficiency. Certain antiretroviral medications have also been linked to borderline riboflavin deficiency, which can result in acute lactic acidosis. The clinical manifestations of riboflavin deficiency include a sore throat accompanied by redness and swelling of the mucosa in the mouth and throat. Other symptoms include cheilosis and angular stomatitis, which present as cracking of the lips and corners of the mouth, as well as glossitis, characterized by a magenta-colored tongue with atrophy. Seborrheic dermatitis or pseudo-syphilis may occur, presenting as moist, scaly skin, particularly affecting the scrotum, labia majora, and nasolabial folds. Additionally, individuals may develop normochromic normocytic anemia, which is characterized by a reduced red blood cell count with normal cell size and hemoglobin content. Riboflavin deficiency often coexists with other nutrient deficiencies, particularly those involving other water-soluble vitamins. In infants undergoing phototherapy for jaundice, increased degradation of riboflavin can occur, potentially leading to deficiency if not carefully monitored. Chronic alcoholism can impair the absorption of riboflavin and other vitamins, such as thiamine, which is associated with conditions like Wernicke's encephalopathy. Studies conducted on the Turkmen population in Iran, who exhibit a significantly higher incidence of esophageal cancer, have suggested a potential link between chronic riboflavin deficiency and the development of esophageal malignancies. Furthermore, riboflavin deficiency has been associated with a sevenfold increased risk of preeclampsia in pregnant women, although the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Pregnant or nursing women are recommended to consume 6 mg of riboflavin per day to meet their increased nutritional needs.
